mcqs.q: Radiation biology is the study of the effects of:
mcqs.explain: Radiation biology studies the effects of ionizing radiation on living systems; the initial interaction occurs within ~10⁻¹³ seconds.

mcqs.q: The 'bystander effect' differs from the older 'hit theory' because it states that radiation damage:
opts: Spreads to neighbouring cells via cell-cell signalling, not only the directly-ionized cell
Affects only the cell directly struck by ionization
Occurs only at very high dose
mcqs.explain: Hit theory said only the directly-hit cell is damaged; the bystander effect shows free radicals trigger signalling that also damages neighbouring cells.

mcqs.q: A deterministic radiation effect is one that:
opts: Is certain above a threshold dose, with severity proportional to dose (e.g. radiation mucositis)
May or may not occur, independent of dose
Never depends on the dose received
Only occurs at diagnostic dose levels
mcqs.explain: Deterministic effects are definite/certain above a threshold and their severity rises with dose — e.g. radiation mucositis.

mcqs.q: A stochastic radiation effect (e.g. radiation-induced cancer) is one that:
opts: May or may not develop; probability (not severity) rises with dose, with no threshold
Always occurs above a fixed threshold dose
Has a severity directly proportional to dose
Cannot be caused by diagnostic radiation
mcqs.explain: Stochastic effects 'may' develop — their probability increases with dose but there is no threshold and severity is dose-independent (e.g. cancer).

mcqs.q: In the DIRECT effect of radiation:
opts: The photon/secondary electron ionizes a biologic molecule directly (~1/3 of damage)
Water is ionized to form free radicals
mcqs.explain: The direct effect ionizes the biologic molecule itself, forming a free radical; it accounts for only about 1/3 of the damage.

mcqs.q: The INDIRECT effect of radiation, which causes ~2/3 of the damage, involves:
opts: Radiolysis of water producing H and OH free radicals that then damage molecules
mcqs.explain: The indirect effect ionizes water (radiolysis), forming H and OH free radicals; these cause ~2/3 of radiation damage.

mcqs.q: Which free radical is the most important in causing tissue damage?
mcqs.explain: The hydroxyl (OH) radical formed by radiolysis of water is the most damaging to tissues.

mcqs.q: According to the law of radiosensitivity, cells are MOST radiosensitive when they:
opts: Have a high mitotic rate, future divisions, and are primitive/undifferentiated
Are highly differentiated and never divide
mcqs.explain: Radiosensitivity is greatest in cells that divide rapidly, have many future divisions, and are primitive/undifferentiated (Bergonié & Tribondeau).

mcqs.q: Which cell type is the MOST radiosensitive?
opts: Vegetative intermitotic cells (e.g. basal mucosa, blood precursors)
mcqs.explain: Vegetative intermitotic cells divide regularly with a long mitotic future, making them the most radiosensitive.

mcqs.q: Which cells are the MOST radioRESISTANT?
opts: Fixed post-mitotic cells — neurons, striated muscle, mature RBCs
mcqs.explain: Fixed post-mitotic cells are highly differentiated and incapable of division once mature, so they are the most resistant (neurons, muscle, RBCs).

mcqs.q: Which group of tissues has HIGH radiosensitivity?
opts: Lymphoid organs, bone marrow, testes, intestine, mucous membrane
mcqs.explain: High-radiosensitivity tissues include lymphoid organs, bone marrow, testes, intestine and mucous membrane.

mcqs.q: The most radiosensitive SITE within the cell is the:
mcqs.explain: The nucleus is the most radiosensitive part of the cell, and DNA is the most sensitive target — strand breaks and cross-linking occur.

mcqs.q: A chromosome aberration (radiation before DNA replication, in G1) differs from a chromatid aberration because it:
opts: Affects both arms and is usually not repaired → leads to mutation
Affects one arm and is reliably repaired
mcqs.explain: Chromosome aberration (exposure before replication) affects both arms and is not/improperly repaired, leading to mutation; chromatid aberration (after synthesis) affects one arm and is usually repaired.

mcqs.q: Radiation damage to nucleic acids (DNA) can lead to:
opts: Immediate cell repair with no risk
mcqs.explain: DNA damage — base-pair loss and broken hydrogen bonds — can cause mutation, carcinogenesis and cell death.

mcqs.q: In radiation mucositis, the oral mucosa breaks down because:
opts: Radiosensitive basal cells die by ~the 2nd week, forming a painful pseudomembrane
mcqs.explain: Radiosensitive basal cells die by the end of the 2nd week; the mucosa breaks down into a painful white-to-yellow pseudomembrane (heals in ~2 months).

mcqs.q: Regarding salivary gland radiosensitivity:
opts: Serous acini are more sensitive than mucous, and the parotid is the most sensitive gland
Mucous acini are most sensitive and the parotid is resistant
The ductal system is more sensitive than the parenchyma
mcqs.explain: Serous acini are more radiosensitive than mucous, the parenchyma more than the ducts, and the parotid is the most sensitive gland — leading to xerostomia.

mcqs.q: Xerostomia after radiotherapy promotes rampant caries mainly because of:
opts: Reduced salivary pH and buffering, with a shift to acidogenic flora
mcqs.explain: Loss of saliva reduces pH and buffering and shifts the flora to acidogenic species, decalcifying the teeth.

mcqs.q: Radiation (rampant) caries characteristically affects the:
opts: Cervical region and cusp tips, with dark pigmentation of the crown
mcqs.explain: Radiation caries typically involves cervical/cementum-dentine areas and cusp tips/incisal edges, with dark pigmentation of the whole crown.

mcqs.q: If radiation is delivered AFTER initiation of calcification but during tooth development, the result is:
opts: Tooth malformation, dwarfed teeth and retarded root development
No effect on the developing tooth
mcqs.explain: Radiation during development causes malformation, dwarfed teeth, retarded/arrested root development and failure to form teeth.

mcqs.q: Osteoradionecrosis develops because irradiated bone becomes:
mcqs.explain: Radiation damages the vasculature and destroys osteoblasts/osteoclasts → hypovascular, hypoxic, hypocellular bone that can progress to osteoradionecrosis.

mcqs.q: The single best way to PREVENT osteoradionecrosis is to:
opts: Complete necessary dental treatment/extractions before radiotherapy begins
Avoid all oral hygiene during therapy
Place dentures during the acute reaction
mcqs.explain: Caries removal and atraumatic extraction of hopeless teeth should be done BEFORE radiotherapy; post-radiation surgery is best postponed for months.

mcqs.q: Radiation effects on taste buds typically:
opts: Appear at 2–3 weeks and revert in 2–4 months (zinc may help)
Are always permanent after any dose
mcqs.explain: Taste is affected at 2–3 weeks and usually reverts in 2–4 months; zinc supplementation may help, though very high doses can cause permanent damage.

mcqs.q: Long-term (late) radiation tissue damage depends primarily on damage to the:
opts: Fine vasculature → fibrosis and impaired nutrition → cell death
mcqs.explain: Late effects depend mainly on fine-vasculature damage: capillary degeneration, increased permeability and progressive perivascular fibrosis impair nutrition, leading to cell death.

mcqs.q: Chromatid aberrations (radiation after DNA synthesis) generally:
opts: Affect one arm and are repaired by biologic processes, often going unrecognized
Affect both arms and always cause mutation
mcqs.explain: Chromatid aberrations affect a single arm (exposure in G2/late S) and are usually repaired and unrecognized — unlike chromosome aberrations, which lead to mutation.

saqs.q: Differentiate deterministic and stochastic radiation effects with an example of each.
saqs.a: Deterministic: certain above a threshold, severity rises with dose (e.g. radiation mucositis). Stochastic: may/may not occur, probability rises with dose, no threshold (e.g. radiation-induced cancer).

saqs.q: Contrast the direct and indirect effects of radiation.
saqs.a: Direct: photon/electron ionizes a biologic molecule directly → free radical (~1/3 of damage). Indirect: radiolysis of water → H & OH radicals that damage molecules (~2/3 of damage); hydroxyl is most damaging.

saqs.q: List the cell types from most to least radiosensitive.
saqs.a: Vegetative intermitotic > differentiating intermitotic > multipotential connective-tissue > reverting post-mitotic > fixed post-mitotic (most resistant).

saqs.q: Describe chromatid vs chromosome aberrations and their repair.
saqs.a: Chromatid (exposure after DNA synthesis, one arm) — usually repaired, unrecognized. Chromosome (exposure before replication, both arms) — not/improperly repaired → mutation.

saqs.q: How does radiation affect the salivary glands, and what is the consequence?
saqs.a: Serous acini > mucous; parotid most sensitive; parenchyma > ducts. Progressive fibrosis & parenchymal degeneration → xerostomia, low pH, rampant caries, candidiasis.

saqs.q: Why does radiation caries occur, and where is it typically seen?
saqs.a: From xerostomia, low pH, lost buffering & remineralization, and altered flora. Seen at the cervical region and cusp tips, with dark pigmentation of the crown.

saqs.q: What is osteoradionecrosis and how is it prevented?
saqs.a: Irradiated bone becomes hypovascular, hypoxic, hypocellular → necrosis. Prevent by completing dental care/extractions before radiotherapy and postponing post-radiation surgery.
